title: Gluttony and temperance
hookLine: too much, too fast, too fussy

cards: Esau comes in from the field, starving. His brother Jacob has a pot of red lentil stew on the fire. Esau doesn't even name the dish: "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint."
Jacob names a price: your birthright, the eldest son's inheritance. And Esau, in the moment, can only see the bowl. He swears, he eats, he drinks, he gets up and goes.
The text ends it with one flat line: "thus Esau despised his birthright." A whole future, for one meal, right now.

teach.b: Gluttony sounds like a sin about eating too much, and that's part of it. But some Christian teachers saw more than size in it.
Gregory the Great, a pope and teacher, listed the ways a person can go wrong at the table, and only one of them is quantity.

teach.h: TOO SOON, TOO MUCH, TOO FUSSY.
teach.b: Eating too soon, before the time. Too lavishly, always needing the expensive thing. Too much.
Too eagerly, wolfing it down. And too fussily, where it all has to be just so. Each one makes food the center of the world.
That's what happened to Esau. Hunger is not a sin; he really was faint. But in that moment the bowl got bigger than his family, his future, his promise.

The letter to the Hebrews remembers him exactly that way, as the one "who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright." So what's the opposite? Christian tradition calls it temperance, and it isn't joyless.
When Jesus fed the crowd on the hillside, the Gospel slows down before anyone eats: he took the loaves and the fishes, and "looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake."
The answer to gluttony is less about eating less than about receiving food differently. Paul widens it: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."
That's one reason some Christians begin a meal with a pause, a grace: a set prayer, a few words of their own, or a bowed head for one breath.
The pause puts the bowl back in its place: a gift, not a master.

how: Some Christians say grace before meals, some with a set prayer and some in their own words, and some churches keep fasting days; Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs gluttony with temperance.

o: being overweight, and going on a strict diet
letting food rule you, and receiving it with thanks
eating fancy food, and fasting once a week

games.q: the bowl and the birthright — tap the pairs.
p: listed ways to go wrong at the table
looking up to heaven, he blessed

s: gluttony only means eating too much
Gregory the Great also named eating too soon, too lavishly, too eagerly and too fussily.
before the crowd ate, Jesus looked up and blessed the bread
"looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake." a pause first, then the meal.
he really was faint. the trouble was letting one bowl outweigh his whole future.

games.q: you're Esau, faint from the field. your brother offers you a bowl of red stew, for the price of your birthright. what do you do?
o: ask for bread and water instead.
games.why: he swears, eats, drinks, and goes. the text says, "thus Esau despised his birthright."

practice: Bring to mind your next meal and decide on a small pause at the start: a breath, a few words of thanks, a thought for who grew it, cooked it, carried it. If you pray, you can say a grace you already know.
Then picture the first few bites, slow enough to taste.

wordCard.voice: Gluttony and temperance. Letting food become the center, too much, too fast or too fussy; and receiving it as a good gift, with thanks.

orig.note: Latin: the throat, and the old Latin name for the deadly sin of gluttony.

carryVoice: Your line: eat with thanks. Hunger is no sin; the bowl just isn't the world. Rest well.
